claim_review_spans.R1: Getting a 48 on your very first paper when you are used to doing well at home is a heavy blow, especially when you spent an entire week pouring effort into it. It makes complete sense that you feel frozen right now. But a 48 does not mean you cannot succeed at university in English; it almost always means you were judged against an unwritten rule of the US academic system that nobody explained to you.
claim_review_spans.R2: Before you make any permanent decisions about dropping the class, let’s handle the immediate panic step-by-step.
claim_review_spans.R3: Do not start writing or drop anything until you know what that deadline actually is.
claim_review_spans.R4: 1. Look at the top banner or breadcrumbs of the webpage that says "submit tomorrow at 5 p.m."
claim_review_spans.R6: 3. If it is for your **other class**, close that tab for an hour so it stops distracting you.
claim_review_spans.R7: 4. If it **is** for this class, check whether it is a small checkpoint (like a proposal, outline, or short response) or the full essay.
claim_review_spans.R8: In many education systems around the world, the highest form of respect and good scholarship is to faithfully summarize and explain what the experts said, putting it into your own words.
claim_review_spans.R9: - **Changing the words (paraphrasing)** proves you understand what the author said. In the US, this is considered *background*, not an argument.
claim_review_spans.R10: - **Your own argument (a thesis)** means answering the question: *"So what?"* or *"What do YOU claim about this reading?"* (e.g, "Author A's point works well for X, but fails to consider Y," or "Between these two viewpoints, Approach B is more convincing because...").
claim_review_spans.R11: A mark of 48 usually means the professor gave you credit for reading and summarizing, but deducted marks because there was no thesis or analytical position. **This is a translation of academic culture, not a measure of your intelligence or your English ability.** It is entirely fixable once you know what they are looking for.
claim_review_spans.R12: Wanting to drop the class is an understandable protective reaction—you want the stress and bad feeling to stop. But as an international student in the US, dropping a class has real legal and financial implications:
claim_review_spans.R13: - **Immigration status:** Most student visas require you to maintain "full-time enrollment" (usually at least 12 credit hours for undergraduates). Dropping below full-time without prior, formal authorization from your international student office can jeopardize your legal status in the US.
claim_review_spans.R14: - **Academic recovery:** It is early in the first semester. Many introductory courses have multiple assignments, revision options, or curves, meaning one bad grade early on does not ruin your final course grade.
claim_review_spans.R15: If you find out the assignment due tomorrow at 5 p.m. **is** for this class and you feel completely stuck, send a brief, professional email to the professor today. Professors respect students who communicate early rather than disappearing:
claim_review_spans.R16: > **Subject:** Question regarding [Course Name] and upcoming assignment — [Your Name]
claim_review_spans.R18: > I received the feedback on my first paper ("needs your own argument") and want to make sure I properly understand your expectations. Coming from an educational background outside the US, I realize I focused primarily on summarizing the readings rather than advancing an independent thesis.
claim_review_spans.R19: > I am working on the upcoming assignment, but I want to ensure I am heading in the right direction this time. Would you have 10 minutes during your office hours this week—or a brief moment before/after class—where I could clarify what an effective argument looks like for this prompt?
claim_review_spans.R20: Take a deep breath and check that course tab first. You do not need to figure out your entire semester today—just confirm which class has the deadline tomorrow.
